title: Linux Networking from the Host: Inspecting, Resolving, Testing and Troubleshooting Layer by Layer
intro: Linux host networking is the set of kernel objects and user-space tools (interfaces, addresses, routes, resolvers, sockets and packet capture) that decide how a machine sends and receives traffic, and that you use to find out why it does not. The goal of this lesson is to give you a repeatable, bottom-up method: for each layer from link to application you will learn the exact command, how to read its output, and which failure pattern points to which cause, finishing with a worked diagnosis of a server that cannot reach an API.

sections.heading: Interfaces and addresses: ip link, ip addr and how to read them
sections.content:
An interface is the kernel's handle for one network attachment. It can be a physical NIC (eth0, ens18, enp3s0), a wireless card (wlan0), or a virtual device (lo, docker0, br0, veth..., tun0, wg0). The modern tool is **ip** from the iproute2 package. The older **ifconfig** (net-tools) still appears in old runbooks and is often not installed by default, but it only sees part of the picture: it cannot show multiple address families cleanly, policy routing, or neighbor tables.

The two commands you will use constantly:

```bash
ip -br link          # brief: one line per interface with state
ip -br addr          # brief: addresses per interface
ip addr show ens18   # full detail for one interface
```

Full output looks like this:

```
2: ens18: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 1500 qdisc fq_codel state UP group default qlen 1000
    link/ether 52:54:00:3a:91:0c brd ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff
    inet 10.20.5.14/24 brd 10.20.5.255 scope global dynamic ens18
       valid_lft 85321sec preferred_lft 85321sec
    inet6 fe80::5054:ff:fe3a:910c/64 scope link
```

How to read it, left to right:

- **The flags in angle brackets.** UP means the interface is administratively enabled (someone or something ran ip link set up). LOWER_UP means the layer below, the physical or virtual link, has carrier. These are two different facts. UP without LOWER_UP, with state DOWN or the word NO-CARRIER, means the interface is enabled but nothing is on the other end: unplugged cable, dead switch port, or a disconnected virtual NIC in the hypervisor. No UP flag at all means it is administratively down.
- **state.** The operational state. UNKNOWN is normal for lo and some virtual devices.
- **mtu.** The largest IP packet in bytes the interface sends without fragmenting. 1500 is standard Ethernet; tunnels and some cloud networks use less (for example 1450 or 1420), and an MTU mismatch produces the classic symptom of small requests working while large transfers hang.
- **link/ether.** The MAC address, the layer 2 identity.
- **inet 10.20.5.14/24.** The IPv4 address and prefix length. The /24 tells the kernel which addresses are on this local network. dynamic plus a valid_lft countdown means the address came from DHCP and will expire unless renewed.
- **inet6 fe80::.../64 scope link.** Every IPv6-enabled interface has a link-local address; it is not routable beyond the segment.

Two values are diagnostic by themselves. An address of **169.254.x.x** means the host gave up on DHCP and self-assigned a link-local address, so look at the DHCP server or VLAN. **No inet line at all** means no address was ever configured.

Counters tell you whether the link is healthy under load:

```bash
ip -s link show ens18
```

Rising errors, dropped or overrun values on RX or TX point to a bad cable, duplex mismatch, ring buffer exhaustion or a saturated host.

Changing state at runtime:

```bash
sudo ip link set ens18 down
sudo ip link set ens18 up
sudo ip addr add 10.20.5.15/24 dev ens18
sudo ip addr del 10.20.5.15/24 dev ens18
```

Two warnings. First, these changes live only in the running kernel and vanish at reboot; persistent configuration belongs to NetworkManager (nmcli), systemd-networkd, netplan on Ubuntu, or ifupdown, depending on the distribution. Second, never take down the only interface of a remote machine over SSH unless you have console access, because you will cut off the session that you need to bring it back up.

| Old ifconfig habit | Modern equivalent |
|---|---|
| ifconfig | ip addr, ip -br addr |
| ifconfig eth0 up | ip link set eth0 up |
| ifconfig eth0 10.0.0.5/24 | ip addr add 10.0.0.5/24 dev eth0 |
| arp -a | ip neigh |
| route -n | ip route |

sections.heading: The routing table: how a host decides where a packet goes
sections.content:
Every outgoing packet triggers one question in the kernel: which interface and which next hop? The answer comes from the routing table, which you read with **ip route**.

```
$ ip route
default via 10.20.5.1 dev ens18 proto dhcp src 10.20.5.14 metric 100
10.20.5.0/24 dev ens18 proto kernel scope link src 10.20.5.14 metric 100
172.17.0.0/16 dev docker0 proto kernel scope link src 172.17.0.1 linkdown
```

Read each line as a rule of the form: destination prefix, how to reach it.

- **10.20.5.0/24 dev ens18 proto kernel scope link** is a *connected route*. The kernel created it automatically the moment the address 10.20.5.14/24 was assigned. It says: addresses in this range are on the local wire, so deliver directly using ARP, with no gateway. There is no via keyword.
- **default via 10.20.5.1** is the default route, equivalent to 0.0.0.0/0. It matches anything no more specific route matches, and it sends the packet to the gateway 10.20.5.1, which must itself be on a connected network. proto dhcp tells you who installed it.
- **src** is the source address the kernel will put on packets using that route.
- **metric** breaks ties between routes of equal specificity: lowest metric wins. Two default routes with different metrics, for example Wi-Fi at 600 and Ethernet at 100, is a common source of traffic leaving through an unexpected interface.
- **linkdown** on the docker0 line means the bridge has no active ports; this is normal when no containers run.

The selection rule is **longest prefix match**: the most specific matching route wins, regardless of order in the table. A packet to 10.50.3.7 prefers a 10.50.3.0/24 route over a 10.50.0.0/16 route, and both over the default.

You do not need to do this in your head. Ask the kernel:

```
$ ip route get 93.184.216.34
93.184.216.34 via 10.20.5.1 dev ens18 src 10.20.5.14 uid 1000

$ ip route get 10.20.5.40
10.20.5.40 dev ens18 src 10.20.5.14 uid 1000
```

The first goes via the gateway. The second has no via, which means the destination is on-link and the host will ARP for it directly. This single command settles arguments about which path a packet takes, including which source address and interface.

Adding routes at runtime:

```bash
sudo ip route add 10.50.0.0/16 via 10.20.5.254
sudo ip route replace default via 10.20.5.1 dev ens18
sudo ip route del 10.50.0.0/16
```

Before the packet leaves, the host must know the next hop's MAC address. That is the neighbor table:

```
$ ip neigh show
10.20.5.1 dev ens18 lladdr 00:1c:73:aa:10:01 REACHABLE
10.20.5.40 dev ens18  FAILED
```

REACHABLE and STALE are fine (STALE just means not recently confirmed). **FAILED** or INCOMPLETE means ARP got no reply: the host is off, on another VLAN, or the cable path is broken. If your gateway entry is FAILED, the problem is layer 2, not routing.

The error message itself narrows the cause:

| Message | Meaning |
|---|---|
| connect: Network is unreachable | No route matches the destination; typically the default route is missing |
| No route to host | A route exists, but ARP failed or an ICMP unreachable came back |
| Connection timed out | Packets left but nothing came back (drop, filter, or dead path) |
| Connection refused | The destination host answered with a TCP reset: it is up but nothing listens, or a REJECT rule exists |

Two further notes. A host forwards packets between interfaces only when net.ipv4.ip_forward is 1, which matters for routers, VPN gateways and container hosts. And on multi-homed hosts, *policy routing* (ip rule, ip route show table all) and reverse-path filtering (rp_filter) can silently drop replies that arrive on a different interface than the one the kernel would use to reach the sender.

sections.heading: Name resolution on Linux: hosts, nsswitch, resolv.conf and systemd-resolved
sections.content:
Most network failures reported as 'the network is down' are really name resolution failures. To diagnose them you need to know the real path a name takes.

Applications call the C library function getaddrinfo(). glibc then consults **/etc/nsswitch.conf**, whose hosts line defines the order of sources:

```
hosts: files mymachines resolve [!UNAVAIL=return] dns
```

files means /etc/hosts, resolve means systemd-resolved, dns means the classic resolver reading /etc/resolv.conf. The first source that answers wins. So an entry in /etc/hosts overrides DNS for every program that uses the C library, including ping, curl, ssh and most daemons:

```
127.0.0.1   localhost
10.20.5.30  db01.corp.example db01
```

**/etc/resolv.conf** lists the DNS servers and search behavior:

```
nameserver 127.0.0.53
options edns0 trust-ad
search corp.example
```

nameserver is the server to ask (up to three are used, in order, with a timeout and retry on failure). search appends domains to short names, so ssh db01 is tried as db01.corp.example. The options line can include ndots, which sets how many dots a name needs before it is tried as an absolute name first; Kubernetes pods commonly use ndots:5, which makes a lookup of api.partner.com generate several wasted queries before the real one.

On many modern distributions resolv.conf is not a plain file you edit. It is a symlink managed by systemd-resolved, and the 127.0.0.53 address is a local stub listener. Editing the file will be overwritten. Inspect the real configuration with:

```
$ resolvectl status
Global
       Protocols: -LLMNR -mDNS -DNSOverTLS DNSSEC=no/unsupported
Link 2 (ens18)
    Current Scopes: DNS
         Protocols: +DefaultRoute
Current DNS Server: 10.20.5.2
       DNS Servers: 10.20.5.2 10.20.5.3
        DNS Domain: corp.example
```

This is per-interface, which makes **split DNS** possible: the corporate resolver is asked only for corp.example names (a routing domain, written ~corp.example), while everything else goes to another server. A VPN that adds its own link with its own DNS servers is the usual cause of the symptom 'internal names resolve only when the VPN is up'.

Useful companion commands:

```bash
resolvectl query api.example.com    # resolve through resolved, shows which link and server answered
resolvectl flush-caches             # clear the local cache after a DNS change
resolvectl statistics               # cache hits, transactions, DNSSEC counters
systemctl status systemd-resolved
```

The most important diagnostic distinction is between two tools:

- **getent hosts name** goes through the full NSS path exactly as applications do. It honors /etc/hosts and nsswitch order.
- **dig, host and nslookup** talk to a DNS server directly and ignore /etc/hosts and nsswitch.

This is why a name can work in ping and curl yet return NXDOMAIN in dig, or the reverse. If getent hosts returns an address but dig does not, look for a hosts file entry. If dig works against a server but getent fails, look at nsswitch, resolv.conf, or the resolved link configuration.

What to ask: Which source answered, files or DNS? Which server was asked, and is it the one I expect for this domain? Is a cached answer hiding a recent change?

sections.heading: Querying DNS with dig, host and nslookup
sections.content:
**dig** is the standard tool for asking a DNS server a precise question and seeing its raw answer. A typical query and its output:

```
$ dig api.example.com A
;; ->>HEADER<<- opcode: QUERY, status: NOERROR, id: 41873
;; flags: qr rd ra; QUERY: 1, ANSWER: 2, AUTHORITY: 0, ADDITIONAL: 1

;; QUESTION SECTION:
;api.example.com.               IN      A

;; ANSWER SECTION:
api.example.com.        117     IN      CNAME   api-lb.example.net.
api-lb.example.net.     37      IN      A       203.0.113.25

;; Query time: 23 msec
;; SERVER: 127.0.0.53#53(127.0.0.53) (UDP)
```

Read it in this order:

1. **status** in the header. NOERROR means the query worked. NXDOMAIN means the name does not exist. SERVFAIL means the server could not obtain an answer (upstream failure, broken DNSSEC validation, lame delegation). REFUSED means the server will not answer you (access control).
2. **flags.** qr is a response, rd means recursion was requested, ra means the server offers recursion. aa (authoritative answer) appears only when the server answering owns the zone; its absence means a recursive resolver or a cache answered.
3. **The counts.** ANSWER: 2 tells you how many records came back.
4. **ANSWER SECTION.** Columns are name, TTL, class, type, data. The TTL (117, 37) is the remaining cache lifetime in seconds, and it counts down on repeated queries to a caching resolver. Here the name is a CNAME alias to a load balancer name, and the second record gives the final address. A chain is normal; a CNAME pointing to a name that does not exist is a common misconfiguration.
5. **AUTHORITY SECTION.** Empty on a positive answer. On NXDOMAIN or on NOERROR with zero answers (called NODATA: the name exists but has no record of that type, for example asking for AAAA on an IPv4-only host), it carries the zone's SOA record, whose minimum field controls how long that negative answer is cached (RFC 2308).
6. **Query time and SERVER.** Which resolver actually answered, and how slowly. Slow DNS often looks like a slow application.

Commonly used options:

```bash
dig +short api.example.com             # answer data only, good for scripts
dig api.example.com @1.1.1.1           # ask a specific server, bypassing local config
dig example.com MX                     # record types: A AAAA CNAME MX TXT NS SOA PTR
dig -x 203.0.113.25                    # reverse (PTR) lookup
dig +trace api.example.com             # walk the delegation from the root down
dig +tcp api.example.com               # force TCP, tests whether TCP port 53 is open
dig +noall +answer api.example.com     # print only the answer section
```

The most valuable technique is to **ask two servers and compare**. If the internal resolver returns an address and a public resolver returns NXDOMAIN (or the reverse), you have found split DNS or a stale cache, not a connectivity bug. If all servers agree but the answer is wrong, the record itself is wrong.

Distinguish two failure types:

```
;; communications error to 10.20.5.2#53: timed out
;; no servers could be reached
```

This means you never reached the resolver: routing, firewall, or the server is down. It is a network problem. Compare with status: SERVFAIL, where you did reach the resolver and it failed internally. That is a DNS problem.

**host** and **nslookup** are shorter front ends for quick checks: host api.example.com, host -t MX example.com, nslookup api.example.com 1.1.1.1. They are fine for one-liners, but dig exposes the header, flags and sections you need to reason about, and nslookup is considered legacy on many systems. Remember that none of the three consults /etc/hosts.

sections.heading: Connectivity testing: ping, traceroute, tracepath and mtr
sections.content:
Once an interface, route and name look sane, test whether packets actually flow. Start with **ping**, which sends ICMP echo requests (RFC 792) and times the replies:

```
$ ping -c 4 203.0.113.25
PING 203.0.113.25 (203.0.113.25) 56(84) bytes of data.
64 bytes from 203.0.113.25: icmp_seq=1 ttl=57 time=14.2 ms
64 bytes from 203.0.113.25: icmp_seq=2 ttl=57 time=13.9 ms
64 bytes from 203.0.113.25: icmp_seq=3 ttl=57 time=15.0 ms
64 bytes from 203.0.113.25: icmp_seq=4 ttl=57 time=14.1 ms

--- 203.0.113.25 ping statistics ---
4 packets transmitted, 4 received, 0% packet loss, time 3005ms
rtt min/avg/max/mdev = 13.9/14.3/15.0/0.4 ms
```

What each part tells you:

- **time** is the round-trip time. Compare to your expectation: under 1 ms on the same LAN, 10 to 30 ms within a country, 100 ms or more across oceans. High mdev (jitter) means an unstable path.
- **ttl** is the remaining time-to-live on the reply. Operating systems start at a default (commonly 64 for Linux and macOS, 128 for Windows, 255 for many network devices), and each router subtracts 1. A reply ttl of 57 from a likely initial 64 suggests roughly 7 hops away. It is a hint, not proof.
- **packet loss** matters more as a pattern. Steady 0 percent is healthy; intermittent loss points at congestion, a bad link, or Wi-Fi.

Error messages are diagnostic. 'Destination Host Unreachable' coming *from your own IP* means ARP failed locally; coming *from a router's IP* means that router has no route. 'Network is unreachable' means your own table has no matching route. Pure silence ('100 percent packet loss') means nothing came back, and **silence is ambiguous**.

**ICMP blocked does not mean host down.** Many firewalls, cloud security groups and hardened servers drop echo requests while serving TCP perfectly. So never conclude 'it is down' from a failed ping alone. Test the real protocol instead:

```bash
nc -zv 203.0.113.25 443        # does a TCP handshake complete?
curl -sI https://203.0.113.25 -k --connect-timeout 5
sudo traceroute -T -p 443 203.0.113.25   # trace using TCP SYN to port 443
```

The reverse also happens: ping succeeds but the service is dead, because ping only proves IP-level reachability.

To find *where* a path breaks, use **traceroute**, which sends probes with increasing TTL (1, 2, 3, ...). Each router that decrements TTL to zero returns an ICMP Time Exceeded, revealing itself:

```
$ traceroute -n 203.0.113.25
 1  10.20.5.1      0.4 ms   0.3 ms   0.3 ms
 2  198.51.100.1   2.1 ms   2.0 ms   2.2 ms
 3  * * *
 4  203.0.113.9   13.8 ms  13.9 ms  14.0 ms
 5  203.0.113.25  14.2 ms  14.1 ms  14.3 ms
```

A line of * * * means no reply to those probes: the router filters or rate-limits ICMP. If later hops answer (as here), traffic is clearly passing through it, so it is harmless. If the trace ends in stars forever, the path breaks at or after the last answering hop, but remember the return path can differ from the forward path (asymmetric routing). **tracepath** works without root and also reports the path MTU. **mtr** combines ping and traceroute continuously:

```bash
mtr -rwn -c 50 203.0.113.25
```

In an mtr report, loss that appears at one middle hop but not at later hops is ICMP rate limiting on that router and is not real loss. Loss that begins at a hop and continues to the final destination is real. To test MTU problems, ping with the do-not-fragment flag: ping -M do -s 1472 host. A reply to 1472 bytes (1500 on the wire) but not to larger sizes shows the limit.

sections.heading: Ports and sockets: ss, netstat and lsof
sections.content:
If the host can reach the destination, the next question is whether something is listening on the port, and which process owns it. The modern tool is **ss** (socket statistics), which reads kernel data directly and replaces netstat.

```
$ sudo ss -tulpn
Netid State  Recv-Q Send-Q  Local Address:Port  Peer Address:Port Process
udp   UNCONN 0      0       127.0.0.53%lo:53    0.0.0.0:*         users:(("systemd-resolve",pid=612,fd=13))
tcp   LISTEN 0      4096    0.0.0.0:22          0.0.0.0:*         users:(("sshd",pid=801,fd=3))
tcp   LISTEN 0      511     127.0.0.1:8080      0.0.0.0:*         users:(("nginx",pid=1450,fd=6))
tcp   LISTEN 0      4096    [::]:443            [::]:*            users:(("nginx",pid=1450,fd=7))
```

The flags spell a mnemonic: **t** TCP, **u** UDP, **l** listening only, **p** show process, **n** numeric (no DNS or service-name lookups, which is faster and avoids confusion). Add **a** for all states, and use ss -s for a summary of socket counts by state.

The column that causes the most outages is **Local Address**:

- **127.0.0.1:8080** means only processes on this same host can connect. A remote client will get Connection refused even though the service is running.
- **0.0.0.0:22** means all IPv4 addresses of the host.
- **[::]:443** means all IPv6 addresses, and on Linux this normally also accepts IPv4 (dual-stack) unless the application set IPV6_V6ONLY.
- **10.20.5.14:5432** means only that specific address.

A service listening on loopback while clients connect from elsewhere is probably the single most common 'it works on the server but not from outside' bug. The fix is in the application's bind or listen setting, not the firewall.

On a LISTEN socket, Recv-Q is the current accept queue length and Send-Q is its configured maximum (backlog). A Recv-Q persistently near Send-Q means the application is not calling accept() fast enough, and new connections will be dropped or delayed.

Targeted queries save time:

```bash
sudo ss -ltnp 'sport = :8080'                     # who owns TCP port 8080
ss -tn state established '( dport = :443 )'       # active connections to port 443
ss -tni dst 203.0.113.25                          # per-connection detail: rtt, retransmits, cwnd
```

Process names for sockets owned by other users require root; without it the Process column is empty, which is not the same as 'no process'.

The older equivalents still appear everywhere: **netstat -tulpn** (net-tools) gives similar columns, and **lsof -i :8080** or lsof -iTCP -sTCP:LISTEN -P -n lists open files of type network along with the command and user. **fuser -n tcp 8080** prints the PIDs using the port. Once you have a PID, ps -fp 1450 and systemctl status 1450 tie it back to a service unit.

A classic startup failure is 'Address already in use' (EADDRINUSE). Run ss -ltnp 'sport = :PORT' to find the process that holds the port, then decide whether to stop it or reconfigure one of the two.

The client-side error contrast again points to causes:

- **Connection refused** returns immediately. The host answered with a TCP RST: nothing is listening on that address and port, or a firewall REJECT rule exists.
- **Connection timed out** takes tens of seconds. Packets are silently discarded (firewall DROP, security group, wrong route, dead host).

If ss shows the service listening on the right address yet remote clients cannot connect, inspect the host firewall: sudo nft list ruleset, sudo iptables -S, ufw status, or firewall-cmd --list-all, and then any network firewall or cloud security group between the hosts.

sections.heading: Talking to services: curl, wget, openssl s_client and nc
sections.content:
A port that accepts connections can still serve the wrong thing. Tools that speak the application protocol let you test above layer 4.

**curl** is the workhorse. Its verbose mode narrates each stage, and those stages map directly onto layers:

```
$ curl -sv -o /dev/null https://api.example.com/v1/status
* Host api.example.com:443 was resolved.
* IPv4: 203.0.113.25
*   Trying 203.0.113.25:443...
* Connected to api.example.com (203.0.113.25) port 443
* ALPN: curl offers h2,http/1.1
* SSL connection using TLSv1.3 / TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384
* Server certificate:
*  subject: CN=api.example.com
*  expire date: Mar  3 23:59:59 2027 GMT
* SSL certificate verify ok.
> GET /v1/status HTTP/2
> Host: api.example.com
< HTTP/2 503
< retry-after: 30
```

Read it as a ladder: 'was resolved' proves DNS worked; 'Trying' followed by 'Connected' proves TCP worked (if it stops at Trying, packets are being dropped); the TLS lines show the negotiated protocol and certificate; and the final status line is the application's answer. Here layers 1 to 6 are fine, and the 503 is a server-side problem that retry-after hints is temporary. Knowing exactly how far the ladder got is the entire point.

Useful options:

```bash
curl -I https://api.example.com/health          # HEAD request, headers only
curl -sS --connect-timeout 5 -m 15 URL          # fail fast instead of hanging
curl --resolve api.example.com:443:203.0.113.25 https://api.example.com/
curl -o /dev/null -s -w 'dns=%{time_namelookup} connect=%{time_connect} tls=%{time_appconnect} ttfb=%{time_starttransfer} total=%{time_total} code=%{http_code}' URL
```

The **--resolve** option pins a name to an address, bypassing DNS while keeping the correct Host header and TLS name, so you can separate a DNS problem from a server problem. The -w timing variables show which phase is slow: a large time_namelookup is DNS, a large time_connect is network, a large gap before time_starttransfer is the server thinking.

Status code classes: 2xx success, 3xx redirect (add -L to follow), 4xx client error (401 and 403 are authentication and authorization, 404 wrong path, 429 rate limit), 5xx server error (502 and 504 mean a gateway or proxy could not get a good answer from the upstream). Corporate environments also add proxies; check the http_proxy, https_proxy and no_proxy variables, since a proxy can cause a failure that no direct network test reveals.

Useful curl exit codes: **6** could not resolve host, **7** failed to connect, **28** timeout, **35** TLS handshake failure, **60** certificate not trusted. In scripts these identify the failing layer without parsing text. **wget --spider -S URL** gives similar header-only checking.

For TLS detail, use **openssl s_client**:

```bash
openssl s_client -connect api.example.com:443 -servername api.example.com </dev/null 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer -dates
```

-servername sends SNI; without it a server hosting many sites may return the wrong certificate. Look for 'Verify return code: 0 (ok)'. Code 20 (unable to get local issuer certificate) means a missing intermediate or CA, code 10 means expired, and a name mismatch means the certificate does not cover the host you asked for. Also check the system clock: a skewed clock makes valid certificates look expired.

Finally, **nc** (netcat or ncat) is the simplest port probe:

```bash
nc -zv -w 3 10.20.5.30 5432
# Connection to 10.20.5.30 5432 port [tcp/postgresql] succeeded!
```

-z scans without sending data, -v is verbose, -w sets the timeout. Success means the TCP handshake completed. If nc is not installed, bash can do it: timeout 3 bash -c '</dev/tcp/10.20.5.30/5432' && echo open. UDP checks (nc -zvu) are unreliable because silence is also what an open UDP port looks like.

sections.heading: Watching traffic with tcpdump at troubleshooting level
sections.content:
When tools disagree or report only 'timed out', look at the packets. **tcpdump** captures traffic on an interface and prints one line per packet. At the troubleshooting level you need four habits: choose the interface, filter hard, avoid name lookups, and save to a file when you need a second opinion.

```bash
sudo tcpdump -i ens18 -nn host 203.0.113.25 and port 443
sudo tcpdump -i any -nn port 53
sudo tcpdump -i ens18 -nn -c 200 -w /tmp/api.pcap 'host 203.0.113.25'
tcpdump -nn -r /tmp/api.pcap
```

- **-i** selects the interface (any captures all, but loses link-layer detail).
- **-nn** disables DNS and port-name resolution, which keeps output readable and prevents tcpdump from generating its own DNS traffic.
- **host, net, port, src, dst** build a capture filter in pcap-filter syntax; combine with and, or, not.
- **-c** stops after a count; **-w** writes a pcap file you can open in Wireshark; **-r** reads one back.
- Add -A or -X to see payload as text or hex only when you must, and remember that a capture file may contain credentials and personal data, so handle it accordingly.

Here is what a failing DNS lookup looks like on the wire:

```
14:02:11.120 IP 10.20.5.14.51514 > 10.20.5.2.53: 31877+ A? api.partner-example.com. (41)
14:02:12.121 IP 10.20.5.14.51514 > 10.20.5.2.53: 31877+ A? api.partner-example.com. (41)
14:02:14.122 IP 10.20.5.14.51514 > 10.20.5.2.53: 31877+ A? api.partner-example.com. (41)
```

Three identical queries with increasing gaps and no response: the host is asking, and the resolver (or the path to it) is not answering. Nothing in the application can fix that.

For TCP, the flags column is the story. [S] is SYN, [S.] is SYN-ACK, [.] is ACK, [P.] carries data, [F.] is FIN, and [R] or [R.] is RST.

| What you see | What it means |
|---|---|
| [S] repeated at about 1, 2, 4 seconds, no reply | SYN is being dropped: firewall DROP, security group, bad route, or dead host |
| [S] followed immediately by [R.] | Host is up but nothing listens, or a REJECT rule: Connection refused |
| [S], [S.], [.] then data, then long silence | Handshake fine; the application or a later device is the problem |
| Many [P.] repeated with the same sequence numbers | Retransmissions: packet loss on the path, or MTU blackhole |
| [R] arriving mid-connection | Something (server, firewall, IPS) is tearing the session down |

Two interpretation rules matter. First, capture on the correct side: tcpdump on a server shows packets arriving *before* the host firewall (iptables or nftables) evaluates them, so seeing the SYN arrive but no SYN-ACK leave points at the local firewall or the application, while not seeing the SYN at all points at the network before the host. Capturing on both ends and comparing is the strongest technique. Second, on the sending host you may see 'incorrect cksum' warnings on outbound packets; this is checksum offload to the NIC and is harmless.

Operational care: always use a filter, a count or time limit, and a destination with free disk space. On a busy production server use -c, rotating files with -C and -W, and capture to a file instead of the terminal. Run it as root or with the appropriate capability.

sections.heading: A layered troubleshooting methodology and a worked example
sections.content:
Network faults are found fastest by walking up the stack and stopping at the first layer that fails. Each step either proves a layer healthy, so you never revisit it, or isolates the fault. Change one thing at a time, note what you did, and compare against a known-good host whenever you can.

| Step | Question | Command | Healthy sign | If it fails |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 Link | Is the interface up with carrier? | ip -br link, ip -s link | UP and LOWER_UP, no errors | Cable, switch port, vNIC, driver |
| 2 Address | Do I have the right IP? | ip -br addr | Expected inet and prefix | DHCP, static config, 169.254 address |
| 3 Gateway | Can I reach the next hop? | ip route, ip neigh, ping GATEWAY | Default route present, gateway REACHABLE | Missing route, VLAN, ARP failure |
| 4 Path | Do packets reach beyond my LAN? | ping IP, mtr, traceroute | Replies, sane RTT | Routing, upstream filtering |
| 5 DNS | Does the name resolve, and via whom? | getent hosts, resolvectl query, dig | Expected address | Resolver down, split DNS, hosts override |
| 6 Port | Does TCP connect? | nc -zv, curl -v, ss on the target | Connected | Firewall drop, refused, wrong bind |
| 7 TLS | Is the certificate and protocol OK? | openssl s_client, curl -v | verify ok | Expired, missing CA, SNI, clock |
| 8 Application | Does the service answer correctly? | curl -i, logs | Expected 2xx | App error, auth, rate limit |

**Worked example.** A server, app01 (10.20.5.14), cannot reach the partner API at https://api.partner-example.com. The application log says 'connection error'. Walk the ladder.

**Steps 1 to 3.** ip -br addr shows ens18 UP 10.20.5.14/24. ip route get 1.1.1.1 returns via 10.20.5.1 dev ens18. ip neigh show 10.20.5.1 is REACHABLE, and ping -c 2 10.20.5.1 succeeds. Link, address and gateway are fine.

**Step 4.** ping -c 2 1.1.1.1 gets replies at 9 ms. The path to the internet works, so this is not a general outage.

**Step 5.** Now the name:

```
$ getent hosts api.partner-example.com
$ echo $?
2
$ dig api.partner-example.com +short
;; communications error to 10.20.5.2#53: timed out
$ dig api.partner-example.com @1.1.1.1 +short
203.0.113.80
```

getent exit code 2 means the name was not found. dig to the configured server times out (a network-level failure, not NXDOMAIN or SERVFAIL), while a public resolver answers with 203.0.113.80. Conclusion: the name exists and the host's configured resolver 10.20.5.2 is unreachable from here. tcpdump -i ens18 -nn port 53 confirms repeated queries and no replies. resolvectl status shows the DHCP-provided servers are 10.20.5.2 and 10.20.5.3; a quick check against the second one with dig @10.20.5.3 answers fine. The first resolver is down for this subnet, and the host is slow because it waits out the timeout before trying the second. A temporary fix such as resolvectl dns ens18 10.20.5.3 restores resolution, and the broken server is reported with the dig evidence.

**Step 6.** DNS now works, but the application still fails. Test the port directly, bypassing DNS to keep variables separate:

```
$ nc -zv -w 5 203.0.113.80 443
nc: connect to 203.0.113.80 port 443 (tcp) timed out: Operation now in progress
$ sudo tcpdump -i ens18 -nn host 203.0.113.80
14:11:03.201 IP 10.20.5.14.40912 > 203.0.113.80.443: Flags [S], seq 2819044611, win 64240
14:11:04.221 IP 10.20.5.14.40912 > 203.0.113.80.443: Flags [S], seq 2819044611, win 64240
14:11:06.269 IP 10.20.5.14.40912 > 203.0.113.80.443: Flags [S], seq 2819044611, win 64240
```

A timeout (not a refusal) with SYN retransmissions and no SYN-ACK means the packets are dropped somewhere. The same nc from another subnet's host succeeds. sudo traceroute -T -p 443 -n 203.0.113.80 dies at the second hop, which is the site firewall. Local firewall rules (nft list ruleset) allow outbound 443, so the drop is upstream.

**Conclusion and handoff.** The evidence is specific: the resolver 10.20.5.2 is unreachable from app01's subnet, and outbound TCP 443 to 203.0.113.80 is dropped after the gateway, probably a missing egress allow rule for the partner address. Hand the network team the destination, port, source address, timestamps, the tcpdump lines and the traceroute. A report like that is resolved in minutes, while 'the API is not working' is not.

Two habits keep you honest. Test the thing the application actually does (same name, same port, same user, same proxy settings), because a test that differs from the real path proves nothing. And always ask what changed recently: a new VLAN, a DHCP scope edit, a rotated certificate or a firewall change explains most faults.

quiz.question: On a server, ip addr show ens18 prints <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP> with state DOWN and no LOWER_UP flag, and the interface still has its configured IP address. What does this most likely mean?

options.label: The interface is administratively disabled and someone must run ip link set ens18 up
The interface is enabled in software but no carrier is detected, so check the cable, switch port or hypervisor virtual NIC link
DHCP has failed and the interface has self-assigned a link-local address
The MTU is mismatched with the switch, so large packets are being dropped

quiz.explanation: UP means the interface is administratively enabled, while LOWER_UP means carrier is present on the layer below. UP without LOWER_UP and state DOWN is the enabled-but-no-carrier pattern, so the physical or virtual link is the suspect. The administratively disabled option is wrong because the UP flag is present. The DHCP failure option is wrong because it would produce a 169.254 address and does not explain a missing carrier. The MTU option is wrong because an MTU mismatch affects large packets on a working link and does not change the carrier state.

quiz.question: The routing table contains: default via 10.20.5.1, 10.50.0.0/16 via 10.20.5.254, and 10.50.3.0/24 via 10.20.5.8. Where will the kernel send a packet destined for 10.50.3.7?

options.label: Via 10.20.5.1, because the default route is always used first
Via 10.20.5.254, because the /16 route was added before the /24 route
Via 10.20.5.8, because the longest matching prefix wins
It is split between the three gateways, because all of them match

quiz.explanation: The kernel picks the most specific matching route, the longest prefix, and 10.50.3.0/24 is more specific than 10.50.0.0/16 and the default route, so 10.20.5.8 is used. The default route is only a last resort when nothing more specific matches. Order of insertion is irrelevant to route selection. Traffic for a single destination is not split among gateways in this basic configuration; only the metric breaks ties between equally specific routes. You can confirm with ip route get 10.50.3.7.

quiz.question: On a host, ping db01 and curl http://db01 both work because /etc/hosts maps db01 to 10.20.5.30, but dig db01.corp.example returns NXDOMAIN. Which statement best explains this?

options.label: dig queries DNS servers directly and ignores /etc/hosts and nsswitch, while ping and curl use the C library resolver which reads /etc/hosts first
The DNS server is overloaded and dig is failing intermittently, so ping is only succeeding by luck
ping and curl cache DNS answers permanently, so they never ask a DNS server
NXDOMAIN means the host 10.20.5.30 is down, so ping should also fail

quiz.explanation: Applications go through getaddrinfo and the nsswitch order, where files (/etc/hosts) comes before dns, while dig sends a query straight to a DNS server and never reads the hosts file. The overloaded server option is wrong because NXDOMAIN is a definite answer that the name does not exist in DNS, not an intermittent fault. The permanent caching option is wrong because those tools do not cache indefinitely; the hosts file is simply consulted first. The host-down option is wrong because NXDOMAIN is about the name's existence in DNS and says nothing about whether an IP is reachable. Use getent hosts to test the real application path.

quiz.question: A web service runs on port 8443 on a server. From another machine, curl to port 8443 fails instantly with Connection refused. On the server, ss -ltnp shows LISTEN 127.0.0.1:8443 owned by the application. What is the best next action?

options.label: Disable the firewall on the server to see whether it is blocking the connection
Increase the curl timeout, since the service is slow to respond
Add a default route on the client machine pointing to the server
Change the application's listen address to the server's interface address or 0.0.0.0, then retest from the client

quiz.explanation: The service is bound to the loopback address, so it only accepts connections made from the server itself, and a remote connection attempt receives an immediate refusal. The fix is in the application's bind setting. Disabling the firewall is wrong because a firewall DROP would cause a timeout rather than an instant refusal, and it is unsafe. Raising the timeout is wrong because the failure is immediate, not slow. A default route on the client is unrelated because the client already reached the server and received a response.

quiz.question: An mtr report to a destination shows 60 percent packet loss at hop 4, but hops 5, 6 and the final destination all show 0 percent loss. What is the correct conclusion?

options.label: Hop 4 is dropping 60 percent of user traffic and must be repaired before anything works
The destination is intermittently down, because loss at any hop means loss at the end
Hop 4 is rate-limiting its ICMP replies, so this is not real loss because the later hops and the destination are clean
The report is invalid, because loss can never differ between hops

quiz.explanation: Routers often deprioritize or rate-limit the ICMP they generate for themselves, so apparent loss at one middle hop that disappears at later hops is not real forwarding loss: the traffic continued to the destination without loss. Real loss begins at a hop and persists through every following hop to the end. The option claiming hop 4 drops user traffic is contradicted by the clean downstream hops. The intermittently down destination option is contradicted by 0 percent loss at the final hop. The invalid report option is wrong because differing loss between hops is exactly the common ICMP rate-limiting pattern.

RFC 1035, Domain Names - Implementation and Specification: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1035
RFC 2308, Negative Caching of DNS Queries: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2308
